artifacts.description: Chunyanggyo and Woljeonggyo Bridge Sites in Gyeongju are located west of the National Gyeongju Museum and south of Gyochon Hanok Village. According to Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms), in the 19th year of King Gyeongdeok’s reign (760), ‘two bridges, Woljeong and Chunyang, were built over Muncheon, south of the palace.’ Excavation data indicate that the bridge piers and abutments were built with stone, while the deck, spanning over 11 meters between piers, was likely wooden. Wooden beams were placed on stone bracket-shaped supports, creating a cantilevered structure. It is highly probable that the bridge had a roof, as lotus-shaped ornaments, charred wood, and roof tiles were found at the Woljeonggyo site. However, no such evidence was found at Chunyanggyo. If the deck was wooden, a roof would have been essential to prevent decay. The pavilion of Chunyanggyo was reconstructed based on excavation findings and Woljeonggyo’s restoration plans, with expert consultation.

artifacts.description:
The Lecture Hall Site at Inwang-dong Temple Site in Gyeongju is about 10m north of the Main Hall Site. Only part of the eastern foundation platform and two rows of southern foundation stones, including two round column bases, were identified. The western side was severely disturbed, making the exact outline unclear.
The site is estimated to be five modules wide at the front and one on the side, with the eastern foundation measuring 22m east-west. Module spacing is 390 cm (front) and 240 cm (sides). Foundation stones range from 120–150 cm in diameter, primarily river stones (10–20 cm), with some cut stones mixed in.
The arrangement and size resemble the Main Hall, leading to its identification as a Lecture Hall. Its depth was inferred to be three modules. Round column bases, stone spacing, and excavated bricks were analyzed with comparative studies, and the final design was completed through expert verification.

artifacts.description:
The bamboo mat discovered at Baesan Fortress in Busan in 2017 was made by peeling off the outer and inner layers of bamboo, flattening them, and then splitting them into thin strips at regular intervals to create the bamboo threads. The length of the bamboo strips reaches 2.5 meters, but their width is only 5 to 6 mm, and the thickness is about 1 mm. There are no bent or broken sections, and even the damaged parts are absent. It can be considered as the 'nano technology' of Silla, a method for reducing the volume and weight of the bamboo mat. 
The bamboo mat from Baesan Fortress underwent restoration and preservation processes and is now stored in the artifact management building of the Busan Museum.

In Samguk Yusa, Volume 42, there is a record of manghye (芒鞋), indicating that the origin of hye (traditional shoes) dates back to before the Three Kingdoms period.
These hye should be considered within the broader category of i (履), along with Goguryeo’s hwanghyeok-ri (黃革履, yellow leather shoes), Baekje’s ohyeok-ri (烏革履, black leather shoes), and Silla’s geumdong-ri (金銅履, gilt-bronze shoes).
Similarly, in the Goryeo period, the national preceptor (guksa, 國師) wore ohyeok-guri (烏革句履, black leather shoes with upturned tips), while commoners wore chori-guri (初履句履, simple leather shoes), both of which can be regarded as types of hye.

artifacts.description:
The South Section of the West Corridor Site in the Temple Site in Inwang-dong, Gyeongju exhibits differences in column base spacing, the presence of foundation stones, and structural characteristics compared to other sections of the West Corridor Site. Based on these distinctions, the site has been divided into two separate buildings: the West Corridor Site and the South Section of the West Corridor Site.
Compared to the northern section of the West Corridor Site, the larger-scale column bases and the smaller bases extending eastward, forming a end module structure, suggest that this area was not a corridor but rather a chamber. Based on these features, the structure was reconstructed accordingly.
The upper structure was reconstructed by synthesizing domestic and international architectural cases and academic research. Through expert consultation and iterative reevaluation, two versions of the architectural model were produced.

artifacts.description:
It's located about 8 meters south of the Pagoda Site.The building is connected to the East and West Corridor Sites through transepts with a double corridor structure on both ends.The basic structure of the building features a cruciform layout, with a central section consisting of four large foundation stones and single-module extensions in the four cardinal directions. The structure includes a central space with large foundation stones, cantilevered sections to the north and south for a saltbox roof, and side chambers extending east and west.
The central section's large foundation stones and the connecting stones between them were set deeply, while the cantilevered section and side chamber foundation stones were positioned more shallowly at around 50 cm. artifacts.description: The Geumdang (Main Hall) Site at Inwang-dong Temple Site in Gyeongju is 6.5 meters north of the Pagoda Site. It is a rectangular structure (19.3m × 15.7m) with a five-by-five module layout. Though all foundation stones were lost, core stone placements and some outer foundation stones were identified. The foundation consisted of long stones (100–150 cm) with finely dressed outer and upper surfaces. Remaining base stones measure 19.4m (north) and 3.4m (east). Excavation data, comparative studies on East Asian architecture, and Silla temple research informed the reconstruction. artifacts.description:
The Building Site 2 in the Temple Site in Inwang-dong, Gyeongju is located between the Main Hall Site and the East Transept. It is a rectangular structure measuring 8.1 meters north-south and 7.5 meters east-west, with a layout of three modules in modules wide at the front and two modules wide at the side.
Although the foundation stones and column bases are missing, the foundation core stones remain. A linear foundation, presumed to be the base of a wall, was identified at the center, corresponding to the main module of the structure. No corresponding building was found on the western side of the Main Hall Site, and the function of Building Site 2 remains unclear. However, its alignment and elevation match those of the Main Hall Site and East Transept, supporting its classification as part of the temple complex.
The superstructure was designed and inferred based on excavation reports, domestic and international cases, and research literature, and was produced after consulting with experts.
